speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP ESTABLISHMENT OF EXPORT FINANCING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great satisfaction in announcing that new and fully adequate export financing facilities are being established. These export financing facilities are being made possible due to the joint initiative of the government and the Canadian chartered banks. Canadian exporters of capital goods will thus be enabled to meet credit competition from foreign suppliers.
For their part, the Canadian chartered banks will operate a new company expressly to provide financing for export transactions on credit terms extending up to five years. Export credits insurance will continue to be made available in support of these operations.
On the government side, support will be given to the financing of export transactions involving credit terms of over five years. The government is prepared to provide guarantees for these extended credit term transactions under section 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act and, in addition, to purchase the guaranteed foreign obligations from the new financing company or other lenders.
Canadian exporters can now seek orders for capital equipment, confident that these new arrangements remove financing impediments that may have deterred them in the past from seeking or obtaining orders abroad. The remaining challenge to Canadian exporters of capital equipment is to be competitive and to find creditworthy buyers.
The complementary facilities to be established by the Canadian chartered banks and the Canadian government is a fine example of effective co-operation between private enterprise and government for the national benefit. Through this important co-operative arrangement, Canadian industry is being given full support to help increase Canadian exports and to stimulate employment in the many key industries that should benefit.
The chartered banks have answered a real need in this unique venture to establish an assured pool of financial resources for export transactions, involving credit to foreign buyers of up to five years. Exporters who have
felt uncertain about the availability of financing in the past and have hesitated to seek foreign business, now have the assured support they need. The Canadian banks have shown this initiative because of a desire to assist Canadian business and help stimulate increasing exports and rising prosperity.
The government's arrangements to permit exporters of capital goods to meet the credit competition of the industrial world are backed by the $200 million already authorized under sections 21 and 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act. It is now a task for exporters to utilize the tools that have been forged for them. Exporters, for their part, must respond with energy and effort to produce goods and equipment of such high quality, and at such competitive prices, that they will sell in the ever enlarging but intensely competitive markets of the world.
It is the sincere hope and expectation of the government that this announcement will be received enthusiastically by both business and labour in Canada, as we know it will be by the Canadian government trade commissioners who are gathering here next week. The trade commissioners are tireless in seeking trade opportunities and in trying to sell Canadian goods. They will welcome these new financial aids that will open new horizons. Business will profit from increasing export orders, not only the contracting exporters but the many dependent suppliers of parts and materials that enter into large capital goods. Labour throughout will benefit from increasing employment in all the industries and regions that profit from rising industrial exports.

Whether it is the intention of the government, by means of this and other measures, to give assistance to secondary industries will remain to be seen as time goes by.
However, in proposing these additional facilities, I want to say that the government is just implementing another suggestion made from this side of the house by the Leader of the Opposition. This suggestion was made during the debate on an amendment to the motion to go into supply on March 21, 1960 when the Leader of the Opposition, dealing in a broad way with matters affecting trade and commerce had this to say, as reported at page 2264 of Hansard for March 21, 1960:
More than ever in this country an expanding volume of exports must be the main objective of Canadian trade policy.

If I have prevented him from making some further concise comment on the substance of the policy announcement, I should be glad to give him the opportunity to finish. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I simply wanted to say that the procedure followed in this instance was similar to that which was followed in the national housing legislation now before us and in the small loans legislation also now before us, in that this policy was one of advancing money to others and implementing in that fashion policies that it seemed to us were not the kind that were requisite to meet the emergency at this time.

The announcement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is one that I think was necessary and, when implemented, should fill an important need. I think hon. members have been aware that Canadian exporters often have been at a disadvantage in comparison with exporters of other nations in that they could not make sales on a credit basis and have available facilities by means of which to cash their commercial paper. As I understand it, provision will now be made for an exporter who sells on a somewhat deferred payment basis to get his money now so that next morning he can go out looking for new business.
I think this move was necessary. I think it is a good move, and I think it was necessary to supplement export credit insurance because I know of instances where sales have been underwritten and guaranteed under the Export Credits Insurance Act and still the money was not available for the completion of the transaction.
We will, of course, study the measure in greater detail when more information is available. However, we think, somewhat


along the line of thinking of the hon. member for Laurier, that we have been promoting this kind of general action when we have advocated an export credit corporation. We think the minister's announcement is worth while and that this provision will be of assistance to Canadian exporters to put them on an equal basis with exporters of other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister. It is based on an article which appears in today's Globe and Mail having to do with some remarks made by the Prime Minister in a speech he delivered yesterday. The statement reads:
We cannot afford indefinitely to exclude almost one quarter of the human race from the areas of major political settlement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister

The statement I made yesterday was:
The aggressive declarations of the leaders of mainland China in tone and content cast a frightening shadow of fear over mankind. Their views are threatening and the necessity of a realistic review of the situation becomes necessary and mandatory... So vast and almost numberless a people cannot be ignored. The world is too interlocked with its common dangers to exclude almost one quarter of the human race from the areas of major political settlement.

I should like very much to be able to read the full statement made by the Prime Minister in this important speech.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, November 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-42, to amend the National Housing Act -Mr. Walker-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a very brief statement which 1 suppose I might describe, in a sense, as collateral to the specific points which are being discussed.
I observed that more than one member of the opposition, in the course of his remarks, referred, as if it were an obvious matter that we all accepted, to the fact that economic conditions are bad. I wish to challenge that suggestion.

National Housing Act
I should like, first of all, to quote some remarks of the hon. member for Nipissing and, second, to quote some remarks of the hon. member for Trinity. These hon. members are, of course, just following some of the very extreme statements made by the Leader of the Opposition to which I shall refer in a moment. The hon. member for Nipissing, just in passing, used these words:
But surely this is not the situation nor the purpose of government policy at the present time, when we are in a recession and when we suffer from a lack of growth momentum.
The hon. member for Trinity went further and said that selling houses was going to be difficult for two reasons. One was interest rates and the other, he said, was because the little man is the man who is most concerned and most upset about the uncertainty in the Canadian economy at the present time.
I have two comments to make about that. I am sorry the hon. member for Trinity is not here. It seems to me that is the kind of statement which is made at random without any real basis for it. I am utterly skeptical about it. I would add: If it were a true picture which I do not believe it is, it would be due to the fact that irresponsible statements are being made by the very people who ought to speak responsibly, including members of parliament. I wanted to refer to these two statements because they were made on the floor of the house. I should like to go on and say that they are following most extraordinary statements made by the Leader of the Opposition.
The Leader of the Opposition, for whom I have great respect, usually speaks with moderation and even with almost a certain gentleness in his tone. I can only say, as I have said before in the house, that occasionally the Leader of the Opposition seems to me like a strong temperance man who has taken one drink too many, and then he is away to the races; he does not care what he does. That is the only way I can explain the extraordinary statements made by the Leader of the Opposition the other day at a meeting of the Ontario women's Liberal association. I am quoting from an article in the Globe and Mail which is entitled "Glooming and Gloating".
An editorial?

Yes. It comments on the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition at a meeting of the Ontario women's Liberal association. I might interject here, in case I should forget later, that there were some much more moderate and much wiser remarks made by the new lady member from

whom we have not heard as yet. However, that is by the way. I turn now to the Globe and Mail, which says:
Again, Mr. Pearson said that unemployment was one of two problems-the other being dominion-provincial fiscal relations-that were pulling down the Diefenbaker government. He said, with obvious relish: "Collapse is not too strong a word." With equal relish, he went on to declare that no government had ever gone down so fast and so far. Even in the dust and heat of party politics, such statements are far-fetched-and unworthy of a man like Mr. Pearson.
I feel that myself. I should like to quote further from the editorial:
Does the Liberal leader really want Canadians to think, does he want the outside world to think, that the Canadian government is reeling on the edge of the abyss?
Why not?

I continue:
Nonsense! The Diefenbaker government has its faults-
Its days are counted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

-failings, follies; but it is quite as sound as the St. Laurent government in which Mr. Pearson distinguished himself. The Liberal leader has a perfect right to seek power for his own party, but he should not do it by selling Canada short, by making it appear that the country is poorly governed by a crumbling regime.
While bemoaning the present unemployment in Canada, Mr. Pearson offered no remedies for it; he simply said it was a bad thing, and blamed it upon the government.
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a question at this point?
Yes.
Does the hon. gentleman seriously think that the Leader of the Opposition is selling the country short by criticizing the government of this country in any terms he likes?
Yes, I do.
I suggest that the hon. gentleman read Mr. Drew's speeches.

I am talking about the Leader of the Opposition, for whom I have great respect and who generally speaks with a sense of responsibility. I suggest, as the Globe suggests, that this remark sounds like a man without any sense of responsibility, and therefore I see fit to criticize it. I am sorry to do so when the Leader of the Opposition is out of the house.
As I said, I intend to make my remarks very brief, and should like to put forward one or two indications of realism. I refer the committee to an article in the Winnipeg Free Press, a newspaper which is not noted

for its tenderness toward this government. However, with regard to unemployment, it does use words to the effect that, although unemployment is serious in some places, it exists in the midst of national prosperity. I believe it is desirable to put that on the record because of these remarks which have been made and which obviously, if they are allowed to go unchallenged, might seem to be admitted.
I should like also to quote briefly from a speech made about two weeks ago by an economist for whom I have great respect, Mr. J. R. Petrie, who used to be with the Canada tax foundation but who now is a consulting economist. He reviews the situation since the end of the war and points out that we have had several recessions and booms. Then he says this:
Although the tempo of activity has obviously slowed down, nevertheless we are operating on a very high plateau of over-all activity. This situation, which in my view is still satisfactory, makes one wonder why there is so much discussion about impending disaster. It might be well to have a quick look at the scoreboard so far this year.
At the beginning of the year, economists were predicting a 5 to 6 per cent gain in gross national product. The revenue forecasts made last spring by the Minister of Finance were predicated upon such a rise. Seasonally adjusted GNP was $35.6 billion during the first quarter, up 1 per cent from the preceding quarter. In the second quarter, GNP was $35.0 billion, the first quarter to quarter decline since 1957. It looks now as though GNP for the year might increase by only 1 or 2 per cent. But I ask you-is this disaster? Exports are still strong. In nine months of this year the total has been 8 per cent ahead of the corresponding period last year. The rate of increase in retail sales generally has levelled off, showing only a fractional gain in eight months. Department store sales show a similar pattern. Chain store sales, however, have continued to be strong and are up 5 per cent to this point.
Then he goes on to housing construction. He is very frank about that matter.
Housing construction has been a soft spot, but then this was to be expected. Housing starts this year are down 25 per cent from the same period of 1959.
Of course at the present moment we are taking steps to try to meet that situation which he frankly points out.
I wish to put that statement on record. I suggest quite seriously, notwithstanding the question of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that we are responsible people. I hope that in the remarks which are made there will be a sense of responsibility on both sides.

I shall be glad to do so, Mr. Chairman. Clause 2 simply raises the loan ratio from 90 per cent to 95 per cent in all the different elements in which loans are made, and to 85 per cent instead of 80 per cent on loans for rental housing. In other words, that goes for clause 2, subclauses 1, 2, 3 and 4 which deal with rental housing for home ownership. Subclause 1 dealt with loans to defence workers. They are also eligible for loans for home ownership or for the purchase of semi-detached or duplex houses. Clause 5 enables such owners to receive an increase in such loans similar to that described in subclause 1 for the owner occupied unit and in subclause 4 for the rented unit. I might say, however, that there are very few such loans going through at this time. That stage seems to be pretty well over for the defence workers.
In subclause 6 loans to co-operative housing associations are dealt with. That is something we do not hear a great deal about, but there are co-operative housing associations carrying on, not on too large a scale. The loan amounts available are the same as other loans for home ownership. The increase from 90 per cent to 95 per cent will decrease the down payment by a further $600.
Then under subclause 7 loans to co-operative housing associations are available on semi-detached houses and duplexes when they are for home ownership. This subclause, however, will enable the co-operative housing associations and the eventual owners to secure the benefit of the increased loan ratio on half the lending value, which will decrease the down payment.
Subclause 8 permits the rental unit also to take advantage of the increase in ratio on rental loans from 80 per cent to 85 per cent. This higher ratio would be applied against the remaining half of the lending value, contributing also to a reduction in the down payment. In other words, a person who lives in his own home can get a loan ratio that is increased from 90 per cent to 95 per cent. On rental homes the increase is from 80 per cent to 85 per cent.
Then under subclause 9 of the new legislation the ratios to co-operative housing associations have also been increased by 5 per cent, which is what this subclause really implies. Down payment will be reduced and construction financing probably will be eased.
Then subclause 10 refers to rental housing financed through approved lenders and constructed by entrepreneurs. The increase in loan ratio from 80 per cent to 85 per cent

National Housing Act of lending value is designed to encourage greater participation in the provision of rental housing units under this section of the act. It will also maintain relationship of loan ratio for home ownership similar to that which has been in existence heretofore. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

As I understand the provisions here, the case the minister gave was that a person purchasing a certain house now would be obliged to put up only 5 per cent of the down payment rather than 10 per cent. He gave as an illustration in that given case that the payment would be $600 instead of $1,200. I am not too sure whether the brief suggestion I am going to make will apply to clause 6. However, I understand that yesterday the hon. member for Carleton asked the members on this side of the house whether we had any suggestions to make on this bill. What I have in mind is this. I understand that under the present regulations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation there are provisions for the construction of apartments for old people with low incomes. From the information I have, the restrictions or requirements of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are so severe, and make buildings so costly, that religious or charitable organizations are unable to take advantage of this provision.
According to the present regulations, the apartments must have separate kitchen facilities, and this adds to the cost of the buildings. We have religious or charitable organizations in this country which are in a position to provide special services to look after old people who have moderate incomes or minor physical handicaps. What I suggest is required is the type of apartment which will provide good rooms with running water and even bathroom facilities, but I think such apartments should have community kitchens and community dining rooms; they could be buildings of a motel or hotel type, more or less.
I suggest to the minister that in order to make these provisions practicable the present restrictions should be lifted, and if this is done I am sure there will be many applications presented to C.M.H.C. in connection with accommodation for aged people.

speechtext:

However, clause 6 makes no reference to the subject which the hon. member is discussing at the present time. The clause deals with subsidized housing, while the hon. member is talking about limited dividend projects.
I am glad he did so, however, because I should like to take the opportunity of publicly inviting service clubs throughout Canada to take up the interests of the poor people, the elderly people and the blind people and, as special enterprises, to take upon themselves the building of limited dividend projects. This will not cost the clubs a cent in the long run. All they have to do is to

put up 10 per cent of the cost from the funds they have in hand. We shall put up the other 90 per cent.
As a result of the changes we made, and which I announced some time ago, the interest rate has been reduced from 5J per cent to 5J per cent, which is just one eighth of one per cent more than the rate at which we borrow from the consolidated fund. This is repayable over a period of 40 years, and we shall make it 50 years if necessary. Thus the service club concerned does not really lose anything. It gets back its 10 per cent and when the loan is repaid over, say, 50 years, it has the building for itself. In the meantime it creates for the members of the club a worth-while hobby, a charitable occupation through which the members are helping the poor and employing their extra energies to advantage. I cannot but advocate that every service club across Canada should take upon itself the building of a limited dividend project for poor, aged or blind people who are not as fortunate as are the members of the service clubs themselves.

I appreciate the attitude which the minister has taken on this question. I wish to remind him that in my own constituency I know of two organizations which are prepared to proceed with such construction. The objection is that the present requirements are too stiff and would make the proposed buildings too costly because, as I said, according to the present regulations each apartment would have to have a separate kitchenette or kitchen facilities, which is not practical in the case of the elderly people I have in mind.
These people have to be looked after, and there are no organizations better able to do this than the religious or charitable orders. I have in mind something in the nature of a community home where these people could have the benefit of a community dining room and a community kitchen. Many of these people are not in a position to cook their own meals and look after themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I appreciate the point which the hon. member for Gloucester is making. It may be that our restrictions do present certain difficulties at this time and tend to create units which are, perhaps, better than some people can afford. But we do not want to get down to having communal places where people sleep in dormitories, so we insisted that the apartments should be self-contained units. However, I shall be happy to consider the suggestion which has been made.
May I take this opportunity to pay my tribute to the father of the hon. member for
National Housing Act Vancouver East, who was a pioneer in this field. I understand the son is carrying on the tradition.
I wonder if the minister could say, of clause 6, that paragraphs (a) and (b) are already included in the legislation and that the only real addition is paragraph (c).

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Nipis-sing is correct. The only change is paragraph (c), and the purpose is to extend the government loan to 75 per cent not only for building new units but for rehabilitating older units. Of course this will cost the government and the municipalities much less than building new units. That is the whole purport of the change.

In the same vein, I wonder if we could clear up the relationship between urban redevelopment and urban renewal. Urban redevelopment, as I understand it, involves tearing down existing units and replacing them with new. In that respect the present legislation calls for a contribution by the federal government of 50 per cent toward acquiring the land and property where the redevelopment is to take place. We on this side believe that this process should be further encouraged, and our remarks on this subject yesterday and on previous occasions in other sessions have clearly reflected our thinking on this subject, namely that the contribution of the federal government should be increased from the present 50 per cent to 75 per cent.
I appeal to the minister and through him to the government to give this earnest consideration. I know we cannot move an amendment at this point, for obvious reasons, but we should like to see the figure for the federal contribution increased to 75 per cent.
In connection with the acquisition of existing accommodation, may I say that the provision is a good one and that we support it. However, if slum clearance is not encouraged to the extent I have mentioned there might well be a tendency to renew an area which is really a slum. It is a splendid thing to make greater use of existing stocks of accommodation, but we do not want to create a situation wherein we are encouraging the renewal or protracted use of accommodation that is already in slum condition.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Lambton West.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member for Nipissing, who I thought was taking his seat.

I have one other point to raise, if I may, in connection with the amount of assistance extended in this legislation in

National Housing Act
respect to properties acquired for new construction in slum areas that are being cleared. It is our contention that the legislation at the present time does not go far enough. We would like to see it broadened in scope to include a 75 per cent contribution to sewers, water and streets for these developments. Here again, while it is impossible for us to move an amendment in that regard, we urge the minister to give cosideration to this further degree of assistance, broadening the scope of the government's aid to include these additional services.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether I am in order in raising my questions under this clause, but I do not know under what other clause they could be raised, and if I am not in order Your Honour will draw it to my attention. With respect to the solution to this problem we are facing, may I ask the minister whether it is under regulations or legislation that speculative loans are not available now.
I wish to make reference to a land assembly project in Sarnia to which I referred the other day. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation made available two lots per builder for the purpose of constructing homes commencing this fall. Unfortunately for us there were only 40 lots available in that section. I was wondering whether the minister would consider making this arrangement applicable to the rest of the builders who would like to avail themselves of the opportunity of securing two lots for the purpose of construction beginning this autumn if they could purchase those properties somewhere within the residential area from which people commute to Sarnia for employment.
I think it is important that the government be made aware that today housing accommodation is required not only by people in the city but by people living from 10 to 20 miles away who commute to their employment in the city. I raise this point because a regulation was introduced some months ago to the effect that no building would be permitted in the urban areas where there are no sewage disposal facilities. The effective date of that regulation was postponed to January 1 next. I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to postponing the effective date of that regulation for at least another six months after the first of next year.
I have had some correspondence with the minister on this subject. These regulations naturally become effective overnight, and it would not be proper to have it otherwise. In my own area, where I am familiar with the situation, of course, I know that some of the builders purchased property at a high

price. The property was not serviced by sewers. They were, of course, hoping to build on the property, and found themselves with a great deal of land upon which they could not construct homes. Some were actually faced with bankruptcy. They were relieved to a certain extent by the postponement of that regulation. I urge the minister to seriously consider a further postponement after January 1, 1961. I personally know that some of those who have made a great contribution to our area would be under a terrific financial handicap if they were unable to make use of the property which they purchased at a high price.
Turning now to an area outside the city which could be classified as part urban and part rural, I am wondering where the dividing line is drawn with respect to the requirement for sewage disposal. In my correspondence with the minister I indicated that there are many areas in my riding where there never will be sewage disposal plants, and where as a matter of fact the soil is such that they will not be required because there is a gravel strip-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think perhaps the hon. member's present remarks could be more properly dealt with under clause 36(e), and I would ask him to defer them until we reach consideration of that clause.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I was just about finished anyway. I do not need to outline my point at greater length, except to say that I think consideration must be given to those areas outside a municipality- a city in this case-where such disposal plants will never be built, probably a strip half a mile wide and a few miles long, where the departmental engineers would ascertain to their own satisfaction that there is ample drainage for septic tanks.
Under this clause may I be permitted to ask the minister whether he would consider the feasibility of making loans available under this legislation to the owners of older homes with four or five bedrooms in order that they could acquire smaller homes. It is very difficult to resell homes of that type, especially when they are practically paid for and no mortgage is available. Could consideration be given to amending the act so these people could obtain mortgages and put their homes up for sale. The purchaser would be able to finance the deal under those conditions, and he is unable to do so on any other basis. The vendor could then acquire a new, smaller home. I suggest this is a sound idea to which consideration should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I always value the suggestions of my friend the hon. member

for Lambton West, and I shall be very glad to take his suggestions under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to inquire about the new subclause (c) being inserted in section 36 of the existing legislation. The subclause reads as follows:
(c) the acquisition, improvement and conversion for housing purposes of existing buildings situated in an area specified in an agreement between the province, a municipality in that province and the corporation as an urban renewal area.
Take a specified area on which there is an agreement. If there are historical sites with houses or buildings in it, is the improvement of those houses going to be covered by this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member's question is a very searching one. As he knows, we are primarily interested in providing houses for the poor. However, in redeveloping an area rather than acquiring it, demolishing the buildings and redeveloping it, under paragraph (c) of section 36, we have in mind that if there are any historical houses or monuments in the area we certainly will do nothing to interfere with them. That is particularly true of the province of Quebec. Some have suggested, however, that with respect to lower town and upper town in Quebec there are certain historical parts which are still used for housing. If the city of Quebec in its wisdom came to an agreement with C.M.H.C. to develop and rehabilitate those areas, provided those buildings were used for housing there would be no objection that I can see to their participating in the benefit of this addition to the act.

The minister understood the purpose of my question. I was thinking particularly of the city of Quebec. It may happen that if an agreement is entered into between the province and the municipality and the federal government, there may be historical sites in this area that the city of Quebec would like to keep. If we are improving or renovating this area, I think it would be a good idea also to have those historical sites covered by the act.

Mr. Chairman, you come from Toronto and have a most interesting constituency, but the minister himself has perhaps the most unique constituency in the city of Toronto, ranging as it does from the high class area of Rosedale with all the wealth and prestige it represents down to the heart of cabbagetown, which I suppose is one of the areas that already has some urban renewal planning and where there has been much doing.
Can the minister not illustrate the changes involved in this clause as they would apply in
National Housing Act that particular region? I cannot find, either in his original speech or in any subsequent comments, any clear indication of the scope that is opened up by this addition to the act. Is there a tremendous demand for this urban renewal? Have we a specific example in Toronto which the minister can point out? Would this have anything to do with the Moss park project? I would appreciate the minister's explanation. I know he likes to talk about something which gives him the opportunity to play up Rosedale.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur, who as a student at the university used to deliver beer down in my riding and knows the area well, has a very real point. For instance, in Moss park we have acquired and cleared the land, taken down everything in that area. It was necessary there, as my hon. friend will recall, because if there ever was an area which was what we call blighted it was that area and it needed to be thoroughly demolished, although if it were in Quebec we would not want to have to do that because there are historic spots there which can now be left under this paragraph (c).
In answer to my friend, Moss park was a proper site to acquire and clear out, demolish everything on it, and then start from scratch. But a little further east, in Alexander park, because of the introduction of this legislation, they have been considering the building of a limited dividend project. Now, because of the fact that it is not thoroughly blighted and many parts of it are still very good and blight has only partially set in, it is contemplated, once this becomes law, to rehabilitate some of the old and blighted houses there, probably razing others. Does that give an illustration to my hon. friend?

Yes. The other point I wanted to deal with is this. As the minister has probably heard-I do not think it affects his constituency-Toronto has a termite problem to a certain degree which conceivably, judging by the increasing interest, would indicate that the district would be a prime area for urban renewal. I just wonder whether these alterations would enable the government to step in and work with the municipality and the province in a substantial way in the area along the Danforth from Coxwell where you have this problem, which may be sectionally controlled in one part and not controlled in another part. In other words, my question is how big a scope is envisaged by this method?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
It cannot be a slap-dash job, where we can go along and dab a little here and a little there. The street to which the

National Housing Act hon. member refers is a high class street, and perhaps that would not be the one to use as an example. Let us take Queen street. There are parts of it in the centre of Toronto where we are not suggesting that we just come along and rehabilitate an odd house. This happens to be an area which is badly run down, but not sufficiently to raze it entirely, where you can take the whole area and have an urban renewal program carried on by the rehabilitation of already existing houses as distinct from what we have had to do in urban renewal projects by acquiring the land, razing the buildings and erecting new buildings. It has to be a substantial area.
Would the minister care to indicate exactly the old sites he was talking about that would be covered by the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
If the old sites such as my hon. friend has described in the province of Quebec and which I can visualize, having spent some time there as a student, fulfil the qualifications of the regulations and the act and are situated in an area which is sufficiently run down to necessitate the city of Quebec, in conjunction with the dominion government and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, redeveloping it on the basis of rehabilitation rather than razing and then building anew, then such areas would certainly be considered. But I doubt whether there is anything in the act to permit us to make any grants for the preservation of monuments. My hon. friend will appreciate that there are other sources of funds for that purpose.
We are interested purely in housing, but there may be housing, as my hon. friend knows, in Quebec, very historical houses also, which could be rehabilitated and continued in use as housing. I am not referring to Montcalm's house because that is being used at the present time as a store, but take that as an example. If Montcalm's house were being used for housing at the present time I would think it would be an excellent example. If that area were being used as an urban redevelopment project it would be an excellent example of what we can do under the act. Does that answer my friend?

Yes.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a final question on clause 
6. Is it right that if houses which are considered as historic sites are not used for housing purposes they will not be included under subclause (c)?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is quite right and they also would not be included if they were used as houses unless they were in an area where an urban redevelopment project had been started.
Can the minister inform me if clause 6 provides any further benefits toward the solution of the Trail and district urban redevelopment scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: As I understand it, Trail has a blighted area and has had an urban study made. However, Trail has not yet made application for urban redevelopment. When it does consideration can then be given to the two programs, whether under the old act the properties should be first acquired and then the whole area razed and cleared or whether under the new subclause (c) the buildings that are already there should be rehabilitated.

I understand there has been a rather unusual delay in this matter owing to the difficulty in getting the Canadian Pacific railway to assume a reasonable percentage or possibly the total percentage of the cost of removing their tracks. Would this new legislation provide some assistance in such circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member we will certainly not be making any contribution to the C.P.R. for the removal of their tracks.
Would the minister be good enough to inform the committee what the present position is regarding the land assembly project at St. John's?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not know whether the study there has been completed. St. John's has a very wonderful mayor in Mayor Mews and he is very interested in this matter. The study is in the process of being made at the present time and I think it is almost completed. When the study is completed St. John's will have the same opportunity as Trail to consider which of the two proposals would be most acceptable. Does that answer the question?

The minister will recall that last year he tabled some correspondence about this matter and there were some exchanges in the house about it. At that time the minister made some rather extravagant claims about this project and I should like to read what the minister said as found on page 2141 of Hansard for March 16 last:
I am glad the hon. member-

Referring to the hon. member tor Burin-Burgeo.
-asked his second question. I think very highly of Mayor Mews of St. John's. It is true that we have two law suits pending with the province of Newfoundland, one of them concerning Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have arranged with Mayor Mews-[DOT]
Note these words.
-to have the Royal bank guarante th paymnt for which the province is responsible and, as well, the city of St. John's has made itself responsible so we are no longer dependent on a provincial government upon which we have not been able to depend in the past. We are going ahead at a cost of 75 per cent to ourselves to investigate a very important land assembly project in connection with St. John's where there is a great dearth of housing at the present time.
Those were the minister's own words last March. The minister had personally arranged the financing with the Royal bank, according to his own statement. He recognized there was a great dearth of housing and this thing was going ahead in a great hurry last March. The minister does not seem to know now what is the situation. Perhaps he can enlighten us.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You know, Mr. Chairman, this is another example of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate talking off the top of his head. He is not even talking about the same project.

I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege is that I was not expressing my own words at all. I was reading words that were uttered in this house by the minister and then asking him to account for his own words. I have no doubt whatsoever that the minister was talking off the top of his head when he uttered those words but when the minister comes in here and on his responsibility as a minister of the crown tells this house-*

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what is the question of privilege? My friend is still wrong. He is talking about the wrong thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I should like to hear what is the question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The speechmaking at the banquet is over.
My question of privilege is that the minister was, in a fashion which has now become habitual with him, deliberately misrepresenting something said by someone else in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
If I may tell the Chair why the hon. member is talking off the top of his head, I would point out that he is talking about a land assembly project. He probably does not know the difference between a land assembly project and an urban renewal
National Housing Act development. The land assembly project is not affected by the bill before us today and has nothing to do with the bill. It is something separate. However, for the information of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who knows more about yachts than he does about houses, may I tell him that a land assembly project is one in which a municipality, in this instance St. John's, applies to the federal government for assistance in making an investigation to see whether a certain area designated by them is a proper one for a land assembly project. We subscribe 75 per cent of the cost of that investigation. I appreciate this is the first time my friend has ever heard of it but perhaps I might carry on and explain to him a further distinction between that and an urban redevelopment project.
In so far as an urban redevelopment project is concerned, you take a blighted area and you decide whether it will be acquired, cleared and then built upon or, as under paragraph (c), it will be acquired and then rehabilitated. A land assembly area is designed to be built upon. I hope that the hon. member, perhaps for the first time, appreciates the distinction between the two. Does he? If so I will go on.

The minister having asked me a question, I will answer it. I am most grateful to him for his lecture on the elementary principles of the act, which was not what I was asking about at all and in which I was not particularly interested. The point at issue here is that there is a project under the National Housing Act about which the minister gave certain information and which involved an agreement with the provincial government or an agency of the province. This is the kind of agreement with which this clause deals. The minister gave out certain information about this last March. We want to have that information brought up to date. It is not necessary for the minister to start a diversion about whether it is one kind of development or another kind of development. It is one of those developments which involve an agreement with the province or an agency designated by the province.
Of course the minister did, as all hon. members are well aware, misinform us about one aspect of the matter. In replying to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo last March he said that the city had been designated as an agency of the province when it had not been. However, that was corrected at the last session of the legislature and the city was subsequently designated. I do not use the minister's expression, but he obviously did not know what he was talking about in that respect. He also told the house that he personally had arranged the financing of this
208	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
with the Royal bank. When the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked to have the correspondence on the agreement tabled, it was quite apparent from the returns, which can be examined by any hon. member, that there was no arrangement with the Royal bank made by the minister, nor was there any kind of agreement with the city.
My hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo, and on one or two occasions other hon. members, asked subsequently during the session about this development which had to do, as the minister himself pointed out, with providing housing in a city where the minister said there was a dearth of housing at that time, that is last March. Now when we ask what progress has been made in this matter the minister attempts to divert attention by giving lectures on the act itself. I suggest the minister would do well to address himself to the point before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. You know, patience is a virtue. My hon. friend has been talking about land assembly projects, and I was talking about a land assembly project last March. My hon. friend has cited from Hansard the words I used at that time in connection with the land assembly project. All I said then was correct and all I have said now is still correct. My friend is talking about a land assembly project, and today we should be talking about something entirely different, urban redevelopment.
May I again say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that the land assembly project is still under way in the city of St. John's. Of course, he does not know because he does not keep in touch with Newfoundland the way he should. They are already making a test with 50 acres to determine whether they can buy that property or expropriate it at a price which would justify government money being invested and the land development program being proceeded with, which would enable the citizens of St. John's to purchase lots at a price they could afford. That is going on at the present time. I think they are doing an excellent job. I expressed the belief that it was my fear the people who owned that land may really do themselves out of a deal by asking too much for it.
As I said, a test is being made at the present time on 50 acres to ascertain whether it is worth while proceeding with the plan or whether it is going to be too expensive. Perhaps if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would some day come down to my office I could go over housing with him for an hour so that he may know what he is talking about. It is embarrassing for me to have to come before the committee and point out to him the difference between a land assembly


project and urban renewal development. There is no similarity between the two. If I have answered, and if the hon. member persists in talking about this land assembly scheme about which he apparently has not heard since last March, then, Mr. Chairman, you should make a ruling to confine the lectures he gives here to matters which are relevant to this bill.
May I ask the minister if the land about which he is talking with regard to the development project is included in the land assembly project or is it a separate parcel of land altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Oh, yes, if the project is proceeded with it will comprise more than 50 acres. This particular 50 acres is included in what will be the land assembly project if it should be proceeded with.
May I also say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that we have a letter from the province of Newfoundland, in answer to his contention that I was misleading the committee, appointing the city of St. John's to act as its agent in this land assembly project. I can only rely on the word of the mayor, which has been confirmed by the Royal bank, that in this connection finances have been arranged with the Royal Bank of Canada. Of course, that was necessary under the circumstances since the province of Newfoundland, through no fault of its own but through the instrumentality of Premier Smallwood, has been owing Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation more than $400,000 for a period in excess of a year.

Would the minister say whether the investigation to which he referred at the time this exchange took place in March has been completed, that is the investigation toward which the federal government has contributed 75 per cent of the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It not only has been completed, but as a result of its completion, as I said a moment earlier, the city of St. John's is testing the market on that 50 acres to see if they can go further and commence the land assembly project.
The city has not yet asked the federal government to enter into any agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Pending confirmation of the price of the land and a decision upon whether the matter can be proceeded with, quite naturally the city of St. John's has not proposed signing an agreement when there can be no agreement without a decision on the very important question of the price of the land. Does that answer the hon. member?

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: That is an answer to that question, but I have another question. Can the minister assure the committee that the federal government has the necessary legal power under the existing legislation or that it will have it under this legislation and, if so, in what section, to enter into such an agreement with the city of St. John's, if it desires to do so? speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This discussion is all totally irrelevant to the bill and the amendments to the act. Have I or have I not, Mr. Chairman, your permission to answer? It is completely irrelevant. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Of course the committee is considering clause 6 of the amending bill.
I would say that discussion of the application of the act as it is, when considering the amendment, would not be relevant. But I must say that I have not been able to distinguish between the last question put by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the previous one. Of course, the minister is at liberty to answer if he wishes to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I do so? That is fine.
Perhaps the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will write the hon. member a letter.

Since the minister raises the point, perhaps I might be permitted to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the terms of the new section 36 which clause 6 of this bill purports to put in the act or recommends should be put in the act. It reads as follows:
36. (1) The corporation may, pursuant to agreements made between the government of Canada and the government of any province, undertake jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof projects for
(a) the acquisition and development of land for housing purposes;-
I myself would have thought that those words meant a land assembly project and that what we are doing in this clause is to repeal the present clause 31 and put a new clause 31 in the act just for the precise purpose which the minister in his first lectures
National Housing Act
to me said this clause had nothing to do with.
