speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-agrees with me. I would think that my friend the hon. member for Nipissing also has a considerable advantage over the minister in this regard, judging from the performance we have had from the minister up to now. But it appears that what we are being asked by the government to do in this bill is to re-enact the existing clause and to add a third proviso to it and that therefore the whole clause is before the committee, before we are asked to repeal the existing section 36 and to put a new section 36 in its place. I am sure the Chair would never for a moment consider restricting our discussion of any part of the new section now being asked to be put in the place of the old one.
The new section refers to the acquisition and development of land for housing purposes, that is to say in land assembly projects. It refers to the construction of housing projects for sale or for rent which I presume is the kind of thing that the hon. member for Port Arthur, I think it was, said had gone on in the constituency of the hon. member for Rosedale before the present hon. member for Rosedale occupied his seat in this house and which it is now proposed-and this is the only new part of it-to extend to the acquisition of secondhand houses which may be improved instead of being torn down and replaced.
The questions I am directing are to the first part of this new section 31 which was to take the place of the existing section 31. It has to do with a land assembly project. I am asking the minister if either the existing section 31 or the new section 31 that he proposes to put in its place cloak with power the government or the corporation or both or either, as far as that is concerned, although it would appear to be both, having regard to the language used:
36. (1) The corporation may, pursuant to agreements made between the government of Canada and the government of any province, undertake jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof-
Is the minister satisfied that when this clause has been enacted and this bill has been enacted by parliament, if it is enacted by parliament, the government will have the

National Housing Act
necessary power to make an agreement with St. John's if it wishes to do so or whether some additional power will be required for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would have thought that the banquet last night would have made my friends the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate feel a little bit better than he appears to feel today. In connection with the section to which he was referring, namely section 31, may I say that section 31 of the act has nothing to do with this matter.

I want to correct the minister. I at no time referred to section 31. I referred to section 36. I referred to section 36, part 1. If the minister would look at his bill, he will find it is in front of us.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Tomorrow morning Hansard will differ if my hon. friend does not change it in the meantime. Nine times he referred to section 31. Since my friend is taking his law degree by remote control from Newfoundland and visits that province only long enough in the summer to sail his yacht, may I go over with him section 36 which was enacted when he was a minister of the crown in 1956. The first part of this section 36 was enacted at that time and has not been changed since that time and is not being changed today. May I go over it with him just so he will be able to follow it. If he will just stop making little remarks and will concentrate, if he can, just for 30 seconds, perhaps he will be able to see this. The section reads as follows:
36. (1) The corporation may,-
That is the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
-pursuant to agreements made between the government of Canada and the government of any province, undertake jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof projects for-
My hon. friend is now smiling. He sees it. That is fine. He sees that the provision is "with the government of the province or any agency thereof". The agency is the city of St. John's. The authority has already been given by letter from the minister that the city of St. John's may act as his agent, all under section 36 which was enacted by the government of which my hon. friend was a member. That section, however, makes provision for a land assembly project among other things. But today we are not discussing land assembly projects either at St. John's or any other place. We are discussing urban redevelopment or urban rehabilitation. I will not make any further remarks lest I invite my hon. friend to get on his feet again.

Perhaps the minister, instead of making remarks, would simply

answer the question and thus save himself and the committee a great deal of time. All I am asking the minister is this; and whatever the minister may say, Mr. Chairman, we are discussing whatever may be in these sections. The minister does not make the rules for the House of Commons as to what is to be discussed. The rules are in the rules book. When the government ask us to re-enact a section that is now in the statute, that section is open for discussion in the committee, even though the minister may prefer to have the addition to it discussed. When we are reenacting a bill, any part of the bill is open for discussion. I am not saying any part of the act that is not here is open for discussion. I am saying any part of the bill is open for discussion. This clause reads as follows:
6. Subsection (1) of section 36 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor.
I am asking the minister again whether he is quite satisfied that the new section 36, section 1, part (a), will give to the government the necessary power to enter into this agreement. I must say that it would appear from the language that it would do so but I have not the advantage of the advice of the law officers of the crown as has the minister. I am merely asking whether he is satisfied and the government is satisfied that the necessary power will be there if they wish to enter into that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I sympathize with the minister in regard to this problem. I am not sure whether he understands it completely or whether the hon. member who asked the question understands it. I do not altogether understand it either. Has any consideration been given in connection with the assembly of land to eliminating the abuses which have taken place in the past? I am referring to some of the things which have happened in Toronto and, certainly, to what happened in Sarnia. Every time the government shows any interest in redeveloping an area, speculation becomes rife. Has any consideration been given to solving this problem, either by taxation or other means, whether the renovation of old houses or land assembly programs are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I would point out that paragraph (a) of section 36(1) deals with land assembly; the acquisition and development of land for housing purposes. Paragraph (c), which is the only new part, deals with the acquisition and conversion of housing that already exists. The hon. member for Timis-kaming has raised a very real and important point. As the great development in housing has gone on over the last three years there

Is no question but that a lot of land developers and speculators have grabbed large tracts of land and put up the prices, making it more difficult for the little man to build a house because of the high price he has to pay for a lot. It is with the object of remedying this situation as far as possible that the government has taken advantage of the land assembly part of section 36. At the present time there is a land assembly project under way in the county of Carleton where Borden's farm was some years ago. The property is being bought up, sewers are being put in, and the land divided into lots which are then sold to the public at cost. The difficulty about this is that it can only be carried on on a limited scale and our experience has shown that people line up to buy such lots. Who do you pick? It is only possible to satisfy a certain number of the applicants, and unless such land assembly projects are carried on on a tremendous scale people who are just as entitled to get lots have to be left out.
It is very difficult for us to do anything about land speculation, as the hon. member will appreciate, because once a person has paid money for land he can hold it if he wishes in order to get a bigger price. It is a very difficult thing to deal with, but I would be very happy at any time to hear any suggestions from the hon. member designed to provide the little man with a lot at a reasonable price.

I should like to ask the minister one question on this. Does he see any possibility that this new addition, paragraph (c), is a step along the way toward the position where the National Housing Act and C.M.H.C. will be much more actively engaged in the field of supplying mortgages in respect of the older, used houses? This legislation now seems to open up this prospect in connection with urban renewal plans. If it is good enough for urban renewal, is it good enough for individual renewal of old property?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Individual renewal of property such as this depends on the home improvement section of the act. Individuals may go to the bank and get a loan of up to $4,000. Paragraph (c) does not refer to the matter at all and does not deal with mortgages, but I can assure the hon. member that the government does not contemplate going into the mortgage market or entering it as a lender, or insuring approved loans in respect of older houses, because we have all we can do to keep up with the progress of the new housing.

I am disappointed to hear that. I took it from the tone of a letter I had from the minister a few months ago that he
National Housing Act was interested in this prospect of loosening up the market for housing by permitting mortgage support for older houses. The fact remains that for a great many people it would be much better if they moved into an older house as their first owned home, because the valuations do tend to be lower than those on new homes. However, as the minister knows, the down payment runs to a minimum of half the value of the house. It seems to me that the suggestion I have made would be one way of loosening up the whole market for homes and getting them interchanged. I had hoped this was an indication that perhaps the next step would be to give the same opportunity to those interested in older types of houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur knows that I personally am intensely interested in anything we can do to make house purchasing easier for the little man. It is a matter of funds. An enormous amount of funds is required-one third of a billion dollars last year, for example-which indicates the interest taken in housing by the dominion government.
Clause 6 agreed to.
On clause 7-"University housing project" defined.

I should like to have some information in connection with the definition of university housing projects. The clause reads in part as follows:
"University housing project" means a project undertaken by a university to provide dormitory accommodation for students resident at that university.
I should like to know whether that would include affiliated colleges. In Manitoba we have five or six colleges which give instructions leading to university degrees and these colleges are affiliated with the University of Manitoba. In my constituency we have two colleges, St. Boniface college for boys and St. Joseph's college for girls, and these institutions do have a definite need of borrowing facilities. I should like to know whether they are included in this provision for obtaining loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for St. Boniface for his inquiry. We should like to do everything, we should like to lend money to everybody in this field if we could afford it. Once again, however, it is the taxpayers who have to put up the money for these things, or we have to go to the public market to borrow the money, and there is a limit to the amount we can borrow in order to lend money to the universities. After consultation on this question and having talked the matter over with the

National Housing Act authorities over a long period of time we have reached the decision that we can only deal at this time with the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges- their denfinition of a university and the list they have, which, I think, numbers 37. Any member of the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges is eligible for a loan, provided, of course, that they fulfil the other terms. The hon. member for Port Arthur, for instance, has a college in his constituency. I might ask the hon. gentleman the name of it?
The Lakehead college of arts and sciences.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I know the hon. member is anxious that it should be eligible for a loan to build residences and dormitories. The college has an attendance of 71. He did not tell me how many dormitories he would like built for the 71 students which include men and women. We also have colleges in some of the western provinces with five, seven, 14 students, and so on. It seems a difficult thing to include any school of learning with the name college so we have been forced to accept the definition of the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges and to use their list. I would be very happy to let my friend the hon. member for St. Boniface see the list at any time.

I wonder if the minister could clear up another point for us with respect to this clause. The submission of the university foundation to the Prime Minister last month included a request for legislation such as this for the purpose of constructing residences for students and housing for married students. Is it the intention of the government to have this legislation provide residences and married quarters?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

On the question of universities I appreciate having the comments of the hon. member for St. Boniface. I do not think the minister has been quite fair in his answer in this regard. I intend to move an amendment to this clause of the bill but before doing so wish to make this point.
With respect to Canada Council grants and other kinds of grants for universities the whole situation is to the advantage of the established institutions and yet this is the very time when spokesmen are crying out for the development of new institutions.
I do not know where the minister got the attendance figure of 71 with respect to the Lakehead college. It is higher than that. All these schools are manoeuvring to burst through to university or full college status.


The point is that now is the time they need to set up their facilities and get going. With respect to university grants and Canada Council grants it is a case of "them that has gets". They do not help the new institutions.
I am aware that we have a proliferation of institutions of higher education in Canada. I am also aware that the definition of "university" is a very vague thing; even vaguer is the definition of the word "college". I think it is generally agreed that we know what is an institution of higher education. We know this legislation is designed to help institutions of higher education. For that reason I wish to move;
That clause 7 be amended by inserting after the word "university" in lines 4, 40 and 41, page 3, and line 5, page 4, the phrase "or college of higher education".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I formally put the amendment I should like to hear from hon. members of the committee concerning the validity of this amendment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May we first be provided with a copy of the amendment? I have two different versions here.
I just wrote it out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I know, but there are two different wordings here. We would like to see the copy the chairman has.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Surely.

Mr. Chairman, the question of the validity of the amendment, it seems to me, would rest on the interpretation the minister might give us with respect to certain specific situations. If you grant me permission I should like to cite the case of Alberta. The University of Alberta is located in the wrong city. It is in Edmonton and it should have been located in Calgary, in the first place, but we also now have in Calgary the University of Alberta, Calgary branch, and frankly I am confused as to the status of the Calgary institution. I know it is affiliated with the parent university but it is not a degree-granting institution. It attracts hundreds of students who otherwise would be crowded into the parent organization in the northern city. I should like to hear from the minister as to whether or not the Calgary branch of the University of Alberta would be eligible for this assistance.

It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that those remarks have nothing to do with the validity of the amendment. I think we are agreed that the amendment is valid and in order. It is an attempt on our part to amend the bill. I rise to support the amendment which proposes to extend these loans.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to interrupt to ascertain the view of the committee on the validity of the amendment? It seems to me in some respects that it could be taken as an initiative by a private hon. member to extend treasury expenditure. In this respect I should like to have the views of the committee. Of course, the rule is clear: initiative may come only from a minister of the crown.

Mr. Chairman, may I say a word with respect to the point that Your Honour has raised. It occurs to me, as I am sure it has to other hon. members, that all we are doing here and all the government is asking us to do here is to empower the government to make loans. We do not instruct the government to make loans. The government retains the discretion; it has no obligation whatsoever. All we are doing here is to define the categories of persons and I use the word "persons" in its legal sense. In one way or another what we are doing is to define the category of persons to whom these loans can be made. It does not seem to me, therefore, that this amendment could in any possible way impose any additional charge.
All this amendment seeks to do is to give the government and the corporation a somewhat wider discretion as to the persons to whom these loans can be made. If on the other hand we were allotting a certain sum of money for these loans and the hon. member for Port Arthur had moved an amendment to increase that sum of money I think that would have been beyond his competence or that of any private hon. member, but as long as the government retains its discretion and is asked to lend money to categories of persons other than those included in the bill as it would seem to be provided for in the original wording it would not seem to me to be open to the objection about which Your Honour raises a question.

Mr. Chairman, when I referred to the validity of this amendment I based my statement on the wording of the next clause, "The corporation may with the approval of the governor in council make a loan." All we are doing is giving wider powers of discretion as was mentioned by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say this. In my humble opinion you are right in your interpretation of this matter. It is a matter introduced by a private member by way of an amendment which affects very much indeed the amount to be expended under this bill. If this extra class were included it would increase very greatly the amount of the expenditures and, of course, this money
National Housing Act has to be raised either by loans raised in the public market or by extra taxation. Therefore, I would think that your suggestion would bring an end to the suggested amendment.
In respect of this matter, I say, without at the moment dealing with the important feature which makes it out of order-out of courtesy to the hon. member for Port Arthur -if we added "or college of higher education", what would be the interpretation of that class? Perhaps a group of us could get together tomorrow with the definition we have here and establish a college of higher education.
Will the minister define a university for me?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Medicine Hat asked for a definition of university. May I say that by "university" we understand an institution of higher learning holding this status by provincial statute or royal charter, having the power to confer degrees. In this instance we, as a rule of thumb, are taking cognizance of a list of universities recognized by the national council of Canadian universities.
May I put a question to the minister purely for information. The minister is aware of course because he is a distinguished graduate of the University of Toronto-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Thank you.

-that that university and several others are composed of a number of colleges. It happens that in the case of the University of Toronto most of those colleges are also universities. But in the case of the University of Manitoba, to which I belong, most of those colleges, including St. Boniface college, which was mentioned by the hon. member for St. Boniface, are not universities. If the restricted interpretation given by the minister to this phrasing were to be followed it would mean that only residences erected by the corporations of degree-granting universities, and not those erected by their affiliated colleges, would be eligible for those loans. I cannot believe that that is the intention of the government. I am not seeking to be the least contentious here; I am trying to And out what the real facts are. I would have thought that the purpose of the government in proposing this was to do two things. If I understood the minister's original speech, one was to meet the real need for those additional residences, and the other was to provide as quickly as possible the maximum amount of employment.

National Housing Act
The addition to St. Boniface college, of which I saw the illustration in a newspaper I think only this morning, will provide, for its size, just as much employment as if it had been built by the University of Manitoba. It seems to me, from the point of view the government really has in mind, the minister would not wish-of course, I recognize that definition is not in the act; the minister was just trying to provide us with a convenient definition-to have it restricted in this way.
I admit I am also a little troubled, as the minister was, by the definition that would be given to "college of higher education". But, as I pointed out when we were discussing the point of order, all that this would do, if parliament enacted it in whichever form, would be to give the government the faculty of making those loans. It would not oblige the government to give any loan unless the government, the corporation, or whoever has the final decision in this matter, decided that the institution was a proper subject for the loan. Therefore, it seems to me that, considering that the government is also taking the power that it is asking for under the proposed new section 36D, it will be open to the governor in council, when it is put into the act, to define precisely what kind of institutions will be qualified under this legislation. In a sense, therefore, it might perhaps seem that the hon. gentleman's amendment would be unnecessary. But I think, in order to indicate that parliament really wants-and I am sure the government does, too-these loans to be made to affiliated colleges as well as to the university corporations themselves, if the government could adopt the amendment of the hon. member for Port Arthur, or something perhaps like it or slightly different that would meet the point even more precisely, I think it would better express what we unanimously really want to accomplish in this provision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the first place I think the point of order is well taken. I suggest that a ruling in that connection would dispose of this matter; for if there were to be inherent in the rights of hon. members the right to extend the ambit of expenditures, then indeed the whole basis of constitutional government would end.
However, aside from that question, I should like to refer to the brief that was submitted by the Canadian universities foundation. I am going to start by saying that the opening words are these:
Submission concerning federal grants to Canadian universities and colleges submitted to the Prime Minister of Canada.

Then, it goes on to say in the first paragraph:
The experience of the past 10 years has shown beyond cavil or contradiction the beneficial effects of federal assistance to Canadian universities and colleges.
Further, when it comes to the recommendations, we find on page 10:
That an amendment be introduced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation legislation and regulations to allow the corporation to lend money on 30-year mortgages to the universities at a rate of interest no higher than that paid by the government on its own long term obligations, to permit the universities to construct residences for students and housing for married students.
Further on in the presentation the following appears on page 16:
The construction of student residences has been greatly aided by The Canada Council, but since these grants are available only on a matching basis, it has been difficult to proceed as rapidly as is necessary with the construction of residences. Our fourth request, then,-
That is the one I just read.
-would provide capital for that portion of residence costs not covered by The Canada Council.
The construction of additional student residences is a matter to which the universities are giving serious attention, believing that the advantages of life in residence are no small part of the educational process. For the institutions in small centres of population, more residences are essential if any expansion of numbers at all is to take place. For those in large cities, the only alternative to becoming "commuters' colleges" is to augment the existing residences.
And so it goes.
The average accommodation now available, as reported from 26 Canadian universities and colleges, is only 19 per cent of their student enrolment: barely enough, in other words, for the students from outside the province if they left out those from their own province altogether.
And so it proceeds. We are endeavouring by this particular amendment to answer the request that was made to the extent that it should cover Canadian universities. With respect to the distinctions raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I would say that each one of the colleges to which he makes reference as a college is indeed within the definition of a university. I suggest that there be no alteration made in this clause in the event that you, Mr. Chairman, hold that the amendment is within the authority of a private member. I submit first that it is not and, if you hold to the contrary, that the expansion and extension asked for in the amendment would bring about a condition of affairs in the interpretation of the word "college" which was never intended to be effective and which would mean a tremendous increase in expenditure without the corresponding benefit that all of us desire.

(Translation):

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following
the statement which has just 'been made by the Prime Minister, I should like to say a word or two on the subject of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). The point which has been raised and which the Prime Minister has just dealt with is whether the words which have been added, namely "or colleges of higher education" are of such a nature as to increase the expenditures of the crown, as under the rules of the house, an amendment involving additional expenditures cannot be moved by a private member.
Still on the point of order, it seems to me that in introducing this bill it was the government's intention to include not only universities as such, but also affiliated colleges, such as a great many classical colleges across Canada, not to mention only those existing in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, the mari-times and even in the western provinces.
There is a whole class of colleges to which I think the act should apply. Now the hon. member who has just moved the amendment apparently had some doubts and therefore wanted to clarify the meaning of the word "university". I am no authority on the matter, but I note that the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) is in his seat, and knowing he has dealt in the past with the matter of universities and their definition, I think perhaps he might enlighten the house as to whether or not the word "university" also includes classical colleges across Canada.
If the government's intention was to include in this definition colleges affiliated to universities, then I think the amendment is in order, because it does not increase the expenditures to be incurred by the crown.
I therefore suggest, contrary to the point made by the Prime Minister, that the amendment is in order unless you, Mr. Chairman, or the Secretary of State, can say to the house that the act as it stands includes classical colleges or colleges affiliated to universities.
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I have permitted the discussion to go beyond the strict question of the validity of the amendment because I think the comments on the merits of the amendment have been helpful to me in judging the bearing of the amendment in relation to the general rule that no private member can propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. That principle, of course, is not under discussion.
National Housing Act
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has put forward the view that section 36B only gives authority to the governor in council to make a loan and that therefore the amendment does not in itself increase the amount. I can hardly accept that view because it seems to me that simply the possibility of an increase in the amount would be sufficient to rule the amendment out of order. There is, of course, an obligation on the governor in council to retain some discretion as to the amount of money to be lent for university dormitories and it seems to me that just the possibility of an increase in the amount is sufficient to rule the amendment out of order.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Laurier has explained that in his view the word "university" includes colleges. If it does, the amendment would add nothing and therefore would be out of order for that reason. If, on the other hand, it does add something it seems clear to me that the Chair must take the view that the amendment is out of order because of the principal I have just outlined.
I would refer the committee to paragraph 3 of citation 246, page 207 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, which reads in part as follows:
In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the crown has demanded or recommended a charge.
Therefore if there is any possibility that the amendment enlarges the scope of the terms used in the bill I would think that the Chair has to rule the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to say one word on the ruling you have made? You have indicated that if the word "university" has the meaning which has been suggested by the member for Laurier then the amendment is not necessary. However, we have a definition which has been given to us by the minister and according to my understanding at least it does not include colleges that are affiliated or are otherwise known as classical colleges. What is the true meaning of the word? I am unable to say and I have asked the Secretary of State if he would not help us. He has not replied. I wonder whether the Chair could not give us the meaning so as to indicate whether or not affiliated colleges are covered. If they are, that ends the matter; if they are not, I am certainly going to support the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I took this argument into consideration when I gave my ruling because I explained I did not consider the definition given by the minister. I said that if the word "university" includes colleges, as
216	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act suggested by the hon. member for Laurier, then the amendment is useless and should be ruled out of order on that ground but that if it does add to the term then I certainly must rule that only the crown can take the initiative in asking the house to spend the money of the treasury. Therefore, whatever the view of the hon. member for Laurier is as to the definition which can be given to the term "university" the amendment has to be ruled out of order.

I have here the dominion bureau of statistics publication and reference papers, Canadian institutions of higher education, and how one could clearly put forward the idea that this means it is to be restricted to universities under the definition given by the Minister of Public Works is beyond me. It is far too narrow. I believe the Prime Minister indicated that it was the smaller places that needed the residences, yet this definition plays right into the hands of the largest universities. If the minister would check this publication he would find there are a great number of institutions of higher education in Canada, in terms of numbers not in terms of students, that are not universities.
I cannot, for the life of me, see that the actual word "university" means much. What we want to do is help in developing institutions of higher learning, whether they are in Calgary or St. Boniface or Brandon or, for example, Waterloo college. So far as I know this college does not have university status at this time, yet it has one of the fastest developing engineering schools in the province. It is going to be one of the great colleges in the future. If we are going to have a definition and interpretation which means that the Canadian universities foundation says this is a university, then we are not going to get anywhere. This will be fine for Toronto, McGill and Queen's, but what about these small places that are on the move. I would think that cities such as Regina, Calgary, Port Arthur, Fort William and Sudbury, could get little comfort from this definition. Lord knows, the problem in Quebec is even more severe where they have only two universities.
I should like to point out also that the question of whether a college is degree granting does not mean too much. There are a number of colleges in Canada that have the authority to grant degrees that have not been granting them in recent years. There are others which may have affiliation with older, established universities and which train students for two or three years in university courses, but those students may take their degrees in another place. The importance of residences in these smaller places is just as
[The Chairman.]

great as it is for the big, fat cats of universities. It seems to me we should be very interested to note this move. This means that the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William cannot count on getting any help from this source until they get the provincial government to declare their college a university.
It seems to me that some of the members from Quebec and the maritimes, where there are a lot of colleges and not so many universities, should be disturbed by the limitation in this bill as it has been interpreted by the minister. If the junior colleges are as important as the late secretary of state for external affairs said, then residences for these places are just as valuable, perhaps even more valuable because the students are younger than, on the average, in university courses. There is no sensible reason at all for this limitation unless the minister says the government has not enough money. This seems to be the only answer, that the government has not enough money.
If this program is just going to pump money into the old, established universities I would have thought the older, established universities such as Queen's, which has been building residences on its own for a long period of time, would be in a much better position financially to continue with a program for additional residences than some of the new places that are trying to get going. These are the ones that really need the loans rather than universities. The minister's argument seems to be that it is the old, established institutions that the government can afford to give money to at the present time, and not the newer ones that are getting under way developing.
I should like to point out to the minister, speaking of home territory, that the Lake-head college of arts, science and technology has qualified for a grant from The Canada Council and yet, under the minister's definition, does not qualify under this measure. If The Canada Council is willing to give them a grant toward the building of a fairly elaborate library structure, then it seems nonsensical to me that the government is not willing to lend them some money-it is not giving, it is lending-so that they can consider starting on a most important part of any college or university. I am most disappointed in this interpretation of this section which we have had today. I will be extremely surprised if there are not members in this house from all parties, and especially from Quebec, who are not disappointed at the limitations about which we have learned this afternoon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member who has just taken his seat has said that there are

only two universities in the province of Quebec. I have two in my constituency alone, and I can think of about six.
I was thinking of the two French speaking universities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is another matter that arises, I think, out of this and to which I have given some thought while the discussion has been going on. My remarks are in elaboration of what has been said by the hon. member for Port Arthur. We in this house have on many previous occasions been given a definition of university in connection with other matters. For instance, colleges starting from junior matriculation are included in the definition of university for the purpose of federal grants. Surely it would not be the intention of the government to make a distinction, let alone cause discrimination, between colleges as defined for the purpose of federal grants and colleges or universities as defined by this bill. If there is to be a distinction between those who may apply under this section and those who are entitled to grants under the legislation approved by this parliament earlier, then there is discrimination against the classical colleges; there is discrimination against those institutions of higher learning that are affiliated with universities but are not universities in themselves. I ask the minister and the government to take cognizance of that situation, which is certainly an abnormal one, and which I am sure they would not for one moment want to condone.

I should like to point out that if I understood the Prime Minister and the minister correctly-I am not sure that I did because it seemed to me they were extremely obscure and almost contradictory -I can illustrate my point very easily. In the University of Manitoba there is an institution called United College which has not the power to grant degrees and is not a university. In the University of Toronto the United Church has a college which is called Victoria College and which is part of Victoria University. It has the right to grant degrees, although it does not grant them. If I understand the minister correctly, Victoria College can get loans for its residences and United College in Winnipeg cannot. If that is the intention of the government, then I am against it. I am sure everybody from Manitoba will be against it. I am sure everybody from any other university which is placed in the same situation as Manitoba and has an affiliated college which cannot grant degreees will be against it.
If we misunderstood the minister and he really means to take the definition used for
National Housing Act the purpose of university grants, which includes all those affiliated colleges, then surely we should make that clear in the legislation. We should not leave it to section 36D under which the governor in council may make some order in council that may not appear for a month and, indeed, may not even be passed for months because they will overlook it as they have overlooked the transfer of the various branches of agriculture and northern affairs to the forestry department.
What we should do is to make this bill clear, make clear what we really mean by "university". If we mean university as it is defined in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act-that is not the place for it incidentally but that is where it is now -or if we want to define "university" as it is defined there, it seems to me that it would fairly well cover what the hon. member for Port Arthur had in mind, what those of us on this side of the house had in mind and what I thought the government had in mind but what I was really quite astonished to discover they apparently did not have in mind. But I do not think this situation should be left obscure. If the minister can clear it up I shall be very happy.

I want briefly to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur and others with respect to this proposal. I cannot see the objection from the point of view of the government. The total amount of loans that may be made under this bill is limited to $50 million. All we are asking is that these smaller institutions- and we have a number of them in British Columbia other than the University of British Columbia-which would not be eligible under the bill as it now stands but which are providing a necessary service to outlying parts of the province. We in this group believe in diversification of opportunity for country people as well as for those who live in the larger centres. I wholeheartedly support the amendment that was ruled out of order and the remarks made by those who have spoken previously on this question.

There is one thing here that bothers me in the spirit of what hon. members opposite are attempting to do and it is this. The stated purpose has been for university residences and there is where the great crying need has been. If we get into the realm of colleges, you are going to have to have a book to define what are colleges.
You have it already.

Colleges exist under varying guises in various provinces. There are colleges which are, I may say frankly, no more or

National Housing Act
no less than partly junior high schools and high schools. Is that the purpose of the legislation?
No.

You would have them under the interpretation of colleges of higher learning or higher education. I know some in my own province that go down as low as grade 8, where they take 13-year old students. That is not the purpose of these loans. What we are looking for and it has always been stated and it is certainly in the brief put forward to the government recently, is assistance for universities. Surely we must stick to that assistance. Otherwise we are going to get into trouble. In Alberta we have on the statute books legislation for many junior colleges. Are they to be encompassed in this legislation, or are we going to leave the defining of what are to be covered by this act to some other legislative body? I would suggest to the members of this committee that we stick to what is the definition of a university in the university grants act.
That is what we are asking for.
There are bodies called colleges. I am a graduate of Oxford University; but the degrees which I received were from a college of that university.
No.
I beg to differ with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. It was not the university which granted me my degree.
The hon. member had better read it again.
I will put it to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members of this committee that it is quite clearly understood what are universities and that these loans should be limited to universities.

I just wanted to point out that St. Patrick's College in Ottawa is listed in the d.b.s. reference paper as providing degree courses in arts and science including honours, commerce and social science, professional school of social work leading to masters degree and social work institute and social action. This is a constituent college of the University of Ottawa retaining autonomy of faculty and administration. Could you say that St. Patrick's College is eligible for residences? Does it need them?
I should like to refer the minister to Waterloo college and associate colleges. In one of the seminaries there are several three-year courses leading to a Bachelor of Divinity degree. The other colleges have degree courses 
in arts including honours. The degrees are granted' by the University of Western Ontario with which the college is affiliated and so on. We have all kinds of these arrangements. As a matter of fact in the university college world in Canada we have a fantastic number of different arrangements and affiliations and degree-granting situations.
I followed fairly well the argument of the hon. member who just spoke. It seems to me that it is this. The funds that are available are going to be limited just to universities or what we know as universities. This seems to me to be a great boon for the University of Toronto, Queen's University, Western university or even the new university at Sudbury. However, it is quite likely to mean that a great number of colleges in Canada are going to be running around getting their names changed through provincial charter to universities because actually the name "university" does not mean too much specifically. Traditionally it used to mean an association of colleges or faculties which, I think you will agree, taught a spectrum of knowledge. But today Victoria University, for example, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned, teaches no spectrum of knowledge. It counts on getting the training in science and history and so many other subjects from the university proper. Yet it holds itself out as a university. There is hence a very indistinct line or distinction as to what is a university.
The minister seems to put forward the idea that it is whoever is a member of the Canadian universities foundation. I wonder whether that is exact enough or good enough. For these reasons I wish to suggest to the minister that if he thinks this legislation is going to take until five o'clock he might consider letting this particular clause go and come back to it with perhaps a more concrete or exact definition of just how his officials project the definition and what colleges or universities in Canada would be eligible for this kind of assistance. I know that I want to vote for this part of the bill.
I think it is great. However, I do not want to support it if it is going to have the narrow interpretation that it seems to be getting.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
If the higher education regulation is a narrow interpretation, then we must plead guilty. But this submission has been made by the Canadian universities foundation by the Right Rev. Monsignor Legare, rector of the University of Ottawa and he made it very ably on behalf of the Canadian universities foundation, that an amendment be introduced; and I quote:
That an amendment be introduced to the Central Mortgage and Housing legislation and regulation to allow the corporation to lend money on 30-year

mortgages to universities at a rate of interest no higher than that paid by the government on its long term obligations to permit the universities to construct residences for students and housing for married students.
With the tremendous call on us for loans of this kind, which the monsignor estimated would be in the neighbourhood of $73 million, we are setting up a fund of $50 million in order to start to try to take care of it. After all, there is a limit to what the taxpayers of Canada can afford. There is no discrimination here. All we are trying to do is this: we are thinking of educating the son of the lady on the back concession. It does not matter what university he attends, as long as it is a university where a high degree of education is given, and all we can do, because we are limited in the funds we have, is to back those universities in connection with which there is no question as to their standards. It is not any closed corporation. It is a question of whether those universities qualify to be included in the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges. The United College of Winnipeg, Manitoba, about which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has spoken, is, of course.

I should just like to ask the
minister one question-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
One moment. I should like to finish the answer I am giving. The hon. member has not been entirely quiet. Those institutions qualified to receive assistance would be institutions of higher learning holding this status by provincial statute or royal charter and having the power to confer degrees.
The hon. member for Edmonton West in his able address indicated that there are all kinds of colleges across Canada. Many of them deal with students who enter after the eighth grade, and that is high school standard. If the hon. member for Port Arthur had his way, every institution, provided it wanted to call itself a college, would get a loan.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We only have $50 million here and the Right Rev. Monsignor Legare-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Very Reverend.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The Very Reverend? The rector, let me call him, then, of the University of Ottawa, has pointed out that if this request were granted for these universities of higher education $73 million would be required. Now we have $50 million at the present time, and to be frank with the hon. member for Port Arthur, who seizes on every opportunity to make political
National Housing Act hay-and I do not blame him for doing so -we cannot go any farther at this time.

But how far is the minister going? That is precisely what we are trying to find out. The minister has contradicted himself. He gave a definition of a university just now-it was an institution incorporated by royal or provincial charter and qualified to grant degrees.
Provincial statute.

Very well, incorporated by provincial statute or by royal charter. That includes the University of Manitoba but it does not include United College. On the other hand, he said that in the Ust he had of the national conference United College was included. I have no authority to speak for the hon. member for Port Arthur, but I think he and I are driving at the same thing. Could we be assured that the minister means every institution belonging to the national conference of universities and colleges; that is what we are concerned about. They are the same institutions that get the federal grants. If that is what the government means, why not say so in the act? We do not want high schools to be included in this or, at least, I do not believe anybody does, but we do not want any discrimination against St. John's College or the United College of Winnipeg. I take my own university-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The United College is included.

It is not a university according to the definition the hon. gentleman gave of a university, and when the minister can confuse himself so much in giving an explanation surely we should have the legislation made clear so that the minister may not confuse his colleagues when he comes to make the regulations in the secrecy of the cabinet.

The college in my constituency in which I am particularly interested is affiliated with the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges but it is not a university; at the present time it is not granting degrees. I wanted specifically to see this bill made more specific. It is not a matter of trying to subsidize every high school that wishes to set up some kind of residence. My attempt at amending the definition was not an attempt to get more money spent, particularly. It was to open the way for colleges of higher education.
Having heard the minister's explanation I insist that we are still up in the air regarding which institutions are affected by this bill and we can only fear the worst if the minister bases his argument most of the time on the

National Housing Act
Canadian universities foundation. I have nothing against the foundation, but it is a pressure group, a lobby group formed by the larger Canadian universities to assist them in putting forward their case. That is fine, but it does not cover all the colleges which belong to the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges. They are not identical at all. We find the minister talking about the national conference one minute and about the Canadian universities foundation the next.
I feel the minister has himself been confused about just how far this measure goes. I should like to be able to say to the people in a place such as the lakehead: here is an example of government legislation which you may use if you want it. According to one of the standards here, that is, the national conference, they are affiliated and they will be all right. But if you go by the Canadian universities foundation, the other definition used by the minister, they are out on a limb. Let us have it cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur is always eloquent though not always logical. The national conference of Canadian universities and colleges includes the affiliates of those universities, for instance, the University of Manitoba, of which the United College is an affiliate. The United College is, of course, included. Then there is the University of Toronto, of which the hon. member for Port Arthur is a graduate and it is included in this list of the national conference of Canadian universities with its affiliated colleges-St. Michael's college, Trinity college, Victoria college and so on. There does not seem to be any confusion here.
The national conference of Canadian universities and colleges is made up of universities which pass the test of the definition which we are adopting. I do not see how I can make it any simpler than that. That does include the affiliates where those affiliates are within the purview of the definition I have given. There has already been a ruling on this, Mr. Chairman, and no matter how much I may keep on talking here this is the issue. This is the request we have had. We are complying with the request and we are going as far as we can to satisfy the demands of undergraduates for accommodation in order that they may obtain the best possible education.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to move on to another aspect of this discussion and I make reference now to section 36B, although we are still on clause 7.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I understand we are discussing the individual sections. Perhaps you might continue.

speechtext: We are on clause 7.

speechtext:
Yes, but we are on
section 36A. We are going by sections, I understand.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What I wish to discuss has to do with section 36B and I will reserve my comments until later.

There is one example I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I have here the third annual report of The Canada Council which deals among other things with its university capital grants fund. The council is an institution not directly under the government but it is sponsored by the government and it reports annually to the House of Commons. On page 7 of the report it is indicated that the council may make grants from the university capital grants fund in accordance with the principle and regulations already established and that further consultations with the universities have been held through the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges and the Canadian universities foundation.
On the next page are listed the grants made. One grant was made to Notre Dame College of Nelson, British Columbia, in the amount of $32,700. The Canada Council thought that was a college deserving of a grant of that size which is a large size grant when you consider the size of the institution.
When you examine the register of British Columbia colleges of higher education some information is given about Notre Dame College. It indicates that it offers a two-year course in liberal arts and science from British Columbia junior matriculation. It is affiliated with a college in Spokane, Washington. My question to the minister is this. Notre Dame College qualified and received money. Obviously it was approved by the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges but would it qualify for a loan for residences under this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No, I would not think so.

Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied with the explanation of the minister to the effect that St. Boniface college is included. It was one of the first colleges affiliated with the University of Manitoba, I believe in 1873. There are four or five colleges in greater Winnipeg on the same basis. If United College is included I am satisfied that they will all be included now.

Mr. Chairman, I had not understood at anytime that there was any agreement in the committee that we were going to adopt these proposed new sections of the act separately because they are all

part of a single scheme and they are all comprehended in a single clause of the bill. I did not think there was any agreement to that effect in the committee and I do not think it is desirable under the circumstances. This problem of the definition of a university occurs in 36A and again in 36B. It seems to me we cannot by adopting 36A imply that we are satisfied with it and then seek to do something about 36B. I do not feel the committee should be asked to approve until we have discussed all the new sections and then we should be asked to approve the whole clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Deputy Speaker indicated to me that that is what was suggested. However, it does not make any difference to the Chair. I am agreeable to whatever the committee wishes to do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a situation which I feel is abnormal and which I am sure he would not want to have occur. I will cite the following example. At the college of Rimouski a residence is currently being built for the students of the two last years of the B.A. course. Ostensibly under this legislation this college would not be covered and they could not apply for a loan for the purpose of assistance in that construction. I understand, on the other hand, that the same thing is going on at McGill University and unquestionably that construction would be covered. That is why I say the situation is anomalous. With that end in view, I propose to move an amendment to section 36B, namely:
That section 36(b) be amended as follows:
That after the word "university" in line 5 thereof, there be added the words "as defined for the purposes of federal university grants".

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier is seeking to do what the hon. member for Port Arthur attempted to do earlier by his amendment. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur sought to add the words "or college of higher education" and therefore would have had the effect of extending the limits of the grants. The chairman found that this would have the effect of increasing the amount of money to be spent and ruled against it. The hon. member for Laurier now seeks to do the same thing by changing the words in the draft bill and substituting therefor "as defined for the purposes of federal university grants" which would also have the effect of extending the purview of the grants and would therefore be a matter in which money was involved. The amendment is therefore clearly out of order particularly since my friend the hon. member for Laurier is still in the opposition.
National Housing Act

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two points I should like to make in answer to what the minister says. This amendment will not in any way increase the amount of money expended because that is already taken care of by another portion of the bill which says that the maximum amount which may be loaned is $50 million, so that it would be a question of apportioning the amount under the various clauses. The explanatory note opposite page 3 reads:
The total amount of loans that may be made under this part is limited to $50 million.
The other point I wish to make is this. I understood the minister earlier to say that in giving a definition of "university" what was intended was to follow the list of universities and colleges as defined for federal university grants. The minister will correct me if I am wrong but I understood him to say that a little earlier. If that is the case there can be no objection to this amendment.
In any event I submit with deference that the amendment would not have the effect of increasing the expenditure of the crown in any way. On the contrary, the expenditure of the crown is limited by the $50 million limitation mentioned in the explanatory note opposite page 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I said no such thing. The hon. member for Laurier in his amendment is dealing with some 95 institutions. He would broaden the base of this from 37, as is proposed in the government bill, to 95. It is in connection with this that a member of the opposition, dealing with a money bill, is extending the base on which that money is to be spent, and he knows very well himself that he is out of order. This is a good bill but he would do anything to muddy the waters. He would bring in all these matters.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some observations on the point of order. Since the minister has told us that the institutions he intends to have covered by this bill are all the institutions that belong to the national conference of universities and colleges it so happens these are also the institutions which receive federal grants. If the minister meant what he said, that those institutions were covered by this bill, then all that the amendment my hon. friend from Laurier is moving is doing is to put that in express words in the bill.
When we move this amendment the minister gets up and says that the hon. member for Laurier is seeking to extend the scope of the bill. Do we believe the minister before the amendment was moved or do we believe him after it was moved, because the one position is the exact opposite of the other?

National Housing Act
He says this amendment extends the number of institutions from 38 to 95. If the minister really means that every institution that is eligible for grants, every institution that is a member of the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges, is to be included in this legislation, then this amendment does not increase the scope of the definition at all. If, on the other hand, the government is trying by some kind of subterfuge to cut down the number from 95 to 38, then the government is not being candid. I say that the minister should resolve this point at once.
I admit right off that if in fact the government is seeking to restrict this to 38 institutions and the amendment covers many more institutions, then there is no doubt that the hon. member for Laurier is moving an amendment which would change the purport of the bill, though I still do not think it would be out of order.
If we are to believe the minister, if the minister meant what he said when he said that all the institutions covered by the national conference of universities and colleges are covered, then the amendment of my hon. friend from Laurier precisely defines that, and the government should be glad to be rescued from the ambiguity into which the minister has placed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are not in an ambiguous position. The efforts of my hon. friend, the superb politician, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would make it appear that way, that is all. The hon. member for Laurier, of course, was not in the chamber for part of this debate. At no time did I suggest-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the member for Laurier was good enough to put in my mouth words which I never used. He said that the universities-

I know the hon. member for Laurier would like to annoy me by making those unparliamentary remarks about me. I always consider the source and, after all, one cannot expect very much from the hon. member for Laurier whose whole career as a member for Stormont made it necessary for him to seek election in Laurier where they did not know him.

speechtext: Have I the permission of the committee to do this? I do not know.

speechtext: No, I have not the list of the 95; I have only the list of the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges. I did not raise the question of 95; the hon. member for Laurier did that.

National Housing Act

I want to ask the minister a perfectly legitimate question. In my constituency we have some unincorporated villages which have incorporated corporations for the installation of water systems. Some of these are quite extensive and supply water for a radius of six miles. One of these waterworks corporations in one of these unincorporated villages ma,y decide to install a sewerage system, could they come within the terms of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is a very good question, and we would be glad1 to consider it. We intend to ask that these schemes receive the approval of the province, and if such a scheme as the hon. member describes received such approval, I would think it would qualify for a loan. When the time comes that the regulations are to be drafted we will be glad to keep in mind what the hon. member has submitted.

The minister will recall that when he made his introductory remarks on November 22 I asked him a question. I wanted to know if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the government would be ready to make loans or give subsidies for the construction of main sewers or trunk sewers. The minister in his answer told me that provided a sewage disposal plant is being installed. As I read the definition here of a sewage treatment project it means a project consisting of a trunk sewage collecting system or a central treatment plant or both, In French it reads as follows:
(Translation):
"Sewage treatment project" means a project consisting of a trunk sewage collector system, a central treatment plant or both-
(Text):
I am asking the minister whether I am right in understanding that you can build either a trunk sewer or a main sewer without building a sewage treatment plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: If there is a plant there to take care of it; yes.
But no subsidy will be given for the construction of the sewer, the main collector itself, without a plant to treat the sewage?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No. As my hon. friend will appreciate, what we are trying to do is to eliminate pollution. We intend to make no loans unless there is a sewage disposal plant of some kind; and only if there is such a plant will trunk collector sewers be included.

I understand that the purpose of this act, as it is set out, is to control water pollution and soil pollution. I also understand that the act is to assist with the

construction of houses. I know by experience -and some of the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will remember some cases-of instances in which some cities were prevented from undertaking needed construction of houses in some parts of the city because they had no main sewers. The minister will also recall that this morning the hon. member for Lambton West made the same plea as did the hon. member for Vancouver East. I am therefore asking the minister whether he will not consider also the construction of main sewers without there being an obligation to build a sewage treatment plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The answer is no.

Is there not in this legislation a certain conflict with the winter works program? If a city or municipality borrows $100,000 under the winter works program, the cost of labour will amount to about $10,000. Fifty per cent will be paid by the government for that labour. That means $5,000. If instead of doing that, they come and take advantage of the loan for a project, they can borrow up to two thirds of the amount which will make it $65,000. A quarter of that amount, which is included in the explanatory notes on page 5, will amount to $16,500. If we put in a quarter of the interest, it will be $500. That would mean $17,000 less $5,000. That means that it would cost only $12,000 to the municipality instead of $5,000. In that case it would be advantageous to the municipality to come and borrow for a municipal sewage treatment plant instead of using the winter works program but it would be only for sewage treatment. Then they could go on with the winter works and fire prevention services under the winter works program. Is there not a certain conflict between the two programs?

speechtext: In reply to the hon. member for Hull, may I say that I am no authority on the winter works program. I am just going to ask the minister a question and I might say that I have no point of view on this matter as I did in connection with the previous objection I was making about the universities. cleared first by the Ontario municipal board? Is it a party to the agreement?

speechtext: That is a question of provincial control. It seems to me-and this is a gratuitous answer; it has nothing to do with me or our department-all these matters must be cleared in Ontario, at any rate, by the Ontario municipal board.

I just wanted to raise this matter because I made the point the other day in preliminary remarks that it would be possible since sewage disposal facilities are considered to be local improvements, usually you have money bylaws for them within the municipality. You could create an inequity for the total taxpayers of the municipal corporation if the funds, particularly the rebate half which I am thinking about, went to help a number of people who were paying taxes for local improvements in the section of the city. I would ask the minister this question. From the fact that the Ontario municipal board will have to approve all these projects can we take it that they would be looking after, will I say, the fair position of the ordinary taxpayer in a community as against any advantage that might come to the particular taxpayers?

Does the minister mean that he sees no possibility of any inequity to certain taxpayers under this legislation?

On clause 7.
I have a question to ask the minister and perhaps, since he is a gentleman of the legal profession he will be able to answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Pardon me, I was addressing a few pleasantries to the hon. member for Laurier.
