hardly believe it.

I did want to ask the minister this question. Section 36G mentions that a corporation may "forgive payment by the municipality or municipal sewerage corporation". What is the reason for the use of the

National Housing Act word "forgive" which is usually used in respect to personal relationships where one pardons somebody for what is, perhaps, an offence. Why is that word used in this impersonal relationship?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am just the Minister of Public Works. Perhaps I should submit that question to the Minister of Justice. But this is a common legal term, and the hon. gentleman must have seen it often in wills-under the terms of a will a debt is forgiven or wiped out. It is a legal word as well as a word in common use and it has come down to us through the ancestors of the hon. gentleman since a thousand years ago.

As we said the other day, we are of course, in favour of this legislation in respect to sewage treatment projects but we believe there is a great additional need among the municipalities for long term financing.
With this in mind we proposed back in 1958 a municipal loan fund. Since that time, of course, we have seen greatly increased evidence of the need among municipalities for assistance in long term financing and I hope the minister may give some consideration to this. I know we do not have the ability here to move an amendment designed to increase the charge against the crown, but the need is very great among the municipalities and I hope that further consideration can be given to making more funds available for general purposes in respect of the general projects undertaken by our municipalities.

I have one question I should like to ask, and it concerns an interpretation. This may be clear to other hon. members, but I should like a further explanation. I note that loans may be made "for the purpose of assisting in the construction or expansion of a sewage treatment project". Does this mean that the project must not have been in being; that it must be a new project? That is my first question, and my second question hinges on that. If the project is in being and the municipality desires to expand it because of this bill, is that included?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The answer to the last question is, yes. Expansion is included. The answer to the first question is this: under section 36F the project may consist of new systems, the expansion of existing systems or the replacement of existing systems. Does that answer the hon. member?
Does it apply to a project in being? Suppose a municipality began a project, say, a few months ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Most definitely no, Mr. Chairman.
[Mr. Herridge.l

Supposing there are, say, three municipalities surrounding a town. These municipalities are not able to build a project on their own. Would it be possible under this bill for a project to be undertaken by the three municipalities in combination with the town?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes.

How does the corporation supervise the administration of the loans? How does it ascertain that the municipality or other bodies concerned has complied with the terms of the act? Is there a provision for inspection, or audit?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There will be both inspection and auditing and a similar system has been worked out to that in force in connection with housing, apartments, limited dividend projects and building of that kind.

I am a little uncertain on the matter of storm sewers. From reading the bill I would assume that a combination of storm and sanitary sewers would come within the terms of the measure. However, it would appear that a storm sewer which would run into a river or lake, perhaps would not. I am afraid this would encourage the building of combination sewers which would not be good because you could never have complete sewage treatment from a combined storm and sanitary sewer, which only takes care of about twice the dry water flow; the rest goes into the creek or lake, or whatever it might be. I presume the measure would apply to a combined storm and sanitary sewer which, I think, is a menace, and that it would not apply to storm water sewers which are sewers that take the surplus water away from streets, roofs and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We like to go as far as we can, but in reply to the hon. member for Lincoln, the former mayor of St. Catharines, may I say that we would not pay for any storm sewers. Further, in connection with sewage disposal plants which a municipality might build in combination with storm water sewers, we would only pay for that part of the construction which could be attributed to sewage disposal. Otherwise there would be no limit to the extent of our investment in projects of this kind.

Will there be any priority given to municipalities? I imagine there will be a rush of applications under this measure and I was wondering how the department intends to treat the various applications which come in. In the event that there are not sufficient funds to carry out all the loans, are there to be any priorities set?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
No, we have no priorities in matters of this kind. In housing it is first come first served. Of course, as my hon. friend knows, all these things are subject to the judgment and wisdom of the directors of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. To my mind they have proved themselves to be one of the ablest bodies on the continent ini matters of housing and I hope they will continue to use their good judgment in matters connected with sewage disposal plants.
As my hon. friend will appreciate, they already have some knowledge from their activities in connection with loans for houses in new areas in which sewage disposal plants are being built. First come first served is the rule but there are always circumstances where that might be altered.

Is this a kind of revolving fund in the sense that the money coming back is put back into use again for the same purpose? The fund has a limit of $100 million. We can see the $25 million of it will go as a grant and through rebate $75 million will come back over a period of time. Who does it come back to?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I remember a question was asked a year ago about the money for mortgages under C.M.H.C. Just so no crown corporation can become all powerful and oblivious to the dictates of parliament elected by the people, ever since Charles I, British parliaments have made a point of not giving these crown corporations too much power. In this instance, as with loans for houses, the moneys come back to the consolidated revenue fund. It is not a revolving fund. Does that answer the question?
Yes. That is not the same as with the insurance fund, is it? C.M.H.C. does retain that, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The insurance fund is simply a fund where C.M.H.C. acts as trustee for the beneficiaries under the fund. Perhaps I should have mentioned that yesterday. Out of approximately $3 billion worth of loans, we have in the insurance fund only $70 million which has been collected in premiums. This is a very small sum to be set aside as an insurance fund against such a tremendous investment in mortgages.
Because of the public nature of universities and municipal sewage disposal plants affected by this legislation was it thought unnecessary to have any kind of insurance provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We are dealing here with municipalities, not citizens. We have not felt it necessary to have an insurance fund
National Housing Act in this instance. A sewage disposal plant cannot burn down and a municipality has to continue to exist. Does my hon. friend suggest that we should set up an insurance fund?
I do not know. I was asking just for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In that case the answer is no.

The minister knows that municipalities have different ratings on the investment market. Also their ratings with investment dealers and in various sources I have checked run up and down the scale. I just make the point that you do not have equal risk in terms of municipalities. The minister is aware that some municipalities have been taken over by the provinces in the past. I thought the minister's answer would be that there is no need for insurance because the provinces have a responsibility.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of Labour) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training and to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs of technical and vocational training undertaken under provincial authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs; to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons; to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and incidental matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution introduces legislation to stimulate technical and vocational training and broaden its scope throughout Canada. It is designed to undergird the government's program to increase employment and foster national development.
Canada has never trained enough manpower to meet the needs of its industry. This fact has been underlined again and again in recent studies which my department has been making of changing manpower requirements

Vocational Training
and supplies and their implications for training. To meet our trained manpower needs we have in the past relied on immigration and on the informal acquisition of skill through on the job experience.
Recently we interviewed a cross-section of tradesmen in five skilled occupations and found that about 35 per cent of them had received the greater part of their training outside of Canada. In other words, in five skilled occupations more than one out of every three workers had been trained in another country. Moreover, the more highly skilled the trade or occupation the greater was the dependence on immigration as a source of competent workers. We welcome these newcomers to our country and we appreciate the contribution of their talents and skill. We cannot, however, expect to continue to obtain highly trained people in such numbers.
The second important way in which we have met our trained manpower needs in the past is through informal on the job experience. The process of picking up skill and knowledge informally through job experience has been a factor in the training of Canadians. The study of tradesmen in five key occupations, to which I referred a moment ago showed this very clearly.
I have been talking about the past. The present and the future, I believe, are and will be very different. We are now moving into a situation where we shall have to train, through formally organized programs, a much higher proportion of our manpower than ever before. There are at least three reasons for this. In the first place, during the past decade population in the 15 to 19 years age group rose by a quarter of a million. Yet this is but the beginning of the bulge resulting from the high birth rate of the war and post-war years. In the next five years half a million additional young people will be coming forward for education and training. The further growth during the last half of the sixties will be even greater.
Second, the demand for skilled and technical workers is increasing far more rapidly than employment generally. The fastest growing occupations are those that require high levels of training. These are the occupations that are being pushed to the fore by rapid technological changes. They require a sound fundamental education as a basis for understanding the theory of a particular field of technology. Informal on the job training may adequately supply the techniques required for a specific job but in today's world the skills of workers can rapidly become obsolescent. This is especially serious if the worker's only asset is a knowledge of particular production techniques. It is increasingly necessary for workers to have some understanding

of the field of knowledge basic to their jobs and such knowledge can be acquired only through organized trade and technical training programs.
The third reason why we must train many more people than in the past is that we cannot expect to benefit nearly so much in future from the immigration of skilled and technical workers. Industrial technology is increasing in the countries from which most of these people come with the result that their need is growing as rapidly as ours. Big changes are needed, therefore, in both thought and deed as far as technical and vocational training are concerned.
There are two kinds of training jobs to be done. We must train those already in the labour market who have left the regular school system, particularly the unemployed. We must provide more training for those now in school so that the ranks of the unemployed will not be further increased in the future.
Let me say a word about these two objectives. Our research has shown that there is tremendous diversity in the ways in which people acquire occupational skills. However, formal channels of training leading to recognized levels of achievement are more limited in Canada than in many other countries. In contrast we find that most European countries have well established formal paths which young people can follow to acquire occupational skills. These include arrangements by which people, after leaving school, and I wish to emphasize this point, can improve their education and training in relation to generally recognized standards. Further development of such arrangements is needed in this country.
We need more carefully developed training programs whereby people, after leaving school, could receive sound preparation for careers. If these were available there would not be the same compelling reasons for retaining potential drop-outs within the regular school system at all costs. The development of such arrangements is one of the objectives of this legislation.
The need for more training facilities for those who have left the regular school system is further substantiated by the facts of the present unemployment situation. It has been a cause of deep concern to the government that large numbers of the men and women currently unemployed lack the essential skills to fill jobs that are available. In October, 1960 the rate of unemployment among unskilled workers was almost 15 per cent. This was virtually three times the rate among the rest of the labour force. In other words, the risk of unemployment today for an unskilled person is about three times that for all other

workers. The provision of much more training for these is another objective of this legislation. Already the government has moved in this direction by announcing early last summer that it would meet 75 per cent of the costs of such training when the number of trainees reached an established minimum level.
Technological changes now taking place in industry are putting a premium on highly skilled tradesmen and technical and other specialists. They are some of the key groups on which our industrial efficiency depends. Yet at present about 5 per cent of all young people enrolled in our secondary schools are taking a technical course program. In post-high school technical courses the number of persons enrolled, although increasing considerably, is still only about 8,000. It is another objective of this legislation to expand training facilities for such people.
The success of any vocational or technical training programs depends upon a supply of qualified instructors. It would be a great waste of public funds to provide extensive buildings without providing also for the training of the instruction personnel.
In any expanded program, the training of teachers should be undertaken concurrently with the development of technical training facilities. This means that in Canada a much expanded vocational teacher training program will be necessary. This again is one of the objectives of this legislation.
I have several times referred to the findings of a number of studies which have been made of manpower training needs in this country. Such research provides the basic facts about how the working world is changing. As I have indicated, this research has shown clearly that a large expansion in vocational and technical training must take place in this country. It has also given us important clues as to the kinds of training that need emphasis. We intend to carry on this research through our economics and research branch and our vocational training branch. As in the past, these continuing studies will be under the general direction of the Canadian vocational training advisory council, on which the provincial authorities and others are represented.
As members of the committee know, this council is composed of representatives of employers and organized labour and the provincial governments. Its overview of programs of technical and vocational education in Canada has been an important factor in developments in this field over the years. Moreover, the recommendations of the council support the views of the government as outlined in this legislation.
90205-6-161
Vocational Training
The government has already announced its desire to establish a national productivity council to stimulate industrial efficiency. Greatly expanded training and retraining programs are an essential complement to this action. Since industrial efficiency depends to a great degree upon the skills and technical know-how of our working force, these two proposals stand together. The objectives which it is sought to implement under the authority of this legislation and the financial proposals which will be put forward to the provinces thereunder with parliament's approval constitutes a challenge to us all. In large measure, its success will depend on the vigorous cooperation of the provincial governments.
Through the years we have received excellent co-operation from the provinces in this training field. We now look forward to a much livelier and, we hope, increasingly effective partnership. The adoption of this bill will involve a substantial increase in the federal contribution to the provinces for technical and vocational training. These increases will be reflected in the estimates of the department. The particulars about the provisions of the act and the agreements proposed will be made available at the time of the second reading of this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the experience we have had for two days we were very happy to listen to the serene way in which the Minister of Labour explained his program of vocational training. Because of the unfortunate unemployment situation we will not, at this stage, take the time of the committee by making speeches approving these measures. We want more action for the

Vocational Training
benefit of the unemployed, and less words. The Leader of the Official Opposition stated our intention to adopt this course in the debate on the throne speech. He had given public notice of our intention to do so when he spoke on "The Nation's Business" on November 16, 1960, when he said:
So I propose that we abandon this procedure at this time, in these emergency circumstances; that once the Prime Minister and the two other party leaders have made their policy speeches we stop this general debate, we bring it to an end so that the government can bring down at once its legislative program, including those plans to deal with unemployment, which the Prime Minister said weeks ago he had ready for submission in detail. Surely, any delay in dealing with this problem as we are approaching winter is inexcusable. The time now is for action and not for words.
We do, therefore, approve in principle the present legislation. In the past Liberal governments have always helped the provinces with the construction and maintenance of their technical schools and have helped with vocational training. I know it is the intention of the government to intensify the scope of their action to help to solve the unfortunate problem of unemployment which is growing worse month by month. If we can recall to the Prime Minister his promise that as long as he is Prime Minister nobody will suffer from unemployment, then we have to admit that for the first time the government admits the dangerous situation created by the ever increasing problem. The speech from the throne made no reference to this problem, but this resolution is certainly a step in the right direction because of the great number of young men who are capable of working but who are forced to be idle because of our unstable economy.
When I was in Vancouver about a month ago I was astonished by a press release from the city social service staff which appeared in the Vancouver Sun for Wednesday, October 19. This is what they had to say, and remember this is not the Liberal party, the C.C.F. party or the Social Credit party speaking, but a body completely outside the political field.
Vancouver social service cannot cope with a record flood of single jobless men applying for assistance.
An average of 85 single jobless men line up every day for interviews.
Some wait from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. in the basement corridors of the city health and welfare building only to be turned away.
As a result they miss out on soup line food at skid road hostels and missions.
The present resolution will certainly help the young workers prepare for the future, and this is good. I remember that at the last session I urged the government to make an agreement with the provinces so that we could use some of the facilities of the technical

schools, the arts and trades schools, to give those under 30 years of age receiving unemployment benefits a couple of hours of training every morning. This year the minister brings before us a concrete plan to prepare those workers who have been displaced by automation for other employment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when on May 8, 1959, we met in committee of supply to examine the estimates of the Department of Labour, the member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) spoke at length about automation and the necessity of retraining our young people so as to prepare them to take the jobs available to them provided they have been properly trained for them. Several members took part in the debate on that occasion. Let me mention only a few names in addition to that of the member for Trinity, that is the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), the member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane), the member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), the member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), the member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai).
Going back to page 3470 of Hansard, I note that at that time the minister was far from thinking that the matter was as important as he now claims it to be; he made only a short reference to it, saying "three months and six weeks", during the speech of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.
There you have proof that, on the one hand the government was only recently converted to the idea of more adequate training for our young people who are about to start on their own and, on the other hand, that those who are already out of school or college have to undergo further training the better to serve society and to benefit therefrom.
This seemed new, but ever since 1957, day after day and session after session, we have been repeating to the Minister of Labour and to the government that something special had to be done to keep the economic recession from taking alarming proportions. Every time we were called crepe hangers with no other purpose in mind than frightening people. Nevertheless, at the last session, members of the opposition repeatedly asked for a more complete effort aimed at giving Canadian citizens a chance to fit into jobs that they could fill if they had had a chance to qualify for them. Not until the 23rd and

28th of July did the minister decide to deal with the question of technical training for our young people. From the very start of the last session until July 28, everything was new and commendable. Nothing was required to be done, nothing had to be changed, everything was all right. According to the forecast of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the future held no danger. Prospects were rosy, and we had only hopefully to wait for the days to come. Everything was fine at the time the minister spoke. Yet, shortly after-hardly four months ago-the minister told us that everything was working beautifully and that, in the field of technical training, we should thank those who were working with such devotion in this country. The minister said "Everything is perfect, there is nothing to change, all we have to do is continue".
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think the change is rather abrupt. This year an amendment is being introduced to give a little more scope to the training scheme of our young people who are preparing to enter the labour market and for those who, though already employed, need to improve their skill in order to be more useful to society and to be better treated by society.
I know, however, from the way things have been put to us since the beginning of the session, that the party in power is trying to give the impression that it has created everything, that nothing existed before.
Yet this resolution, as drafted, is almost identical in every respect to the one which has been in the statutes since 1952, when the Liberal party passed the original act and made the first amendments. Only the last few lines are different, and I quote:
... to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and Incidental matters.
That is the only difference. The government's intention, apparently, is only to give additional power to a commission or to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council. We fully approve of that, because we think the government needs advice from important personalities. We entirely agree with the government on that score.
But let no one say that this Is something new, because it is merely a continuation and an improvement-I recognize it-of an existing statute passed by the Liberal party.
I wonder, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) wondered a moment ago,
Business of the House whether the government has had the wisdom to consult with the provinces about this, because even if we were to adopt the legislation, if the provinces find serious objections to it, it would be ineffective.
We admit that education is exclusively a provincial matter. It is only with the agreement of the provinces that we can make the necessary changes.
I wish Quebec members who so loudly protested against Liberal intervention in the field of education stated clearly whether they approve of federal government intervention in the field of education.
We Liberals approve of it provided the provinces agree. We approve of what the government is doing now, as we approved of what the Liberal party did in the past.

Before I ask the acting house leader for the business of the house, perhaps I could be allowed to correct a misstatement which was made by the house leader last night, involuntarily I am sure. As reported at page 187 of Hansard he said as follows:
On Tuesday, in response to the request of the Leader of the Opposition for an early opportunity to discuss international affairs, supported by the member for Vancouver East-who suggested that there should be the earliest possible opportunity for discussing this matter-I am suggesting that we have a debate on external affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier was in the house when the Leader of the Opposition spoke. As reported at page 34 of Hansard, in his opening speech he used these words:
I hope that soon we will have an opportunity to discuss international affairs. During that time X may have some criticism to make about some aspects of our diplomacy at the United Nations and in NATO-
Then, of course, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) subsequently directed this question to me on November 23:
In view of the paramount importance of issues which are now before the fifteenth session of the general assembly of the United Nations, and the international picture, is consideration being given to the earliest possible opportunity for a discussion on the Congo and international policy matters?

Business of the House
To which I replied:
I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman as to the need of a full discussion on the international situation at the earliest possible date. There are many problems which face us today on which it would be most helpful to have the views of parliament.
So the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) suggested it, and it is for that reason, together with the need of a discussion taking place, that we are asking that it should take place on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is true I was in the house when that statement was made, but the Leader of the Opposition made it quite clear that he was asking that the proper priorities be given to the legislation. He felt all along, and he said so, that the legislation which the government had to deal with the emergency should be brought forward at once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: After all, that is what we are doing, but the government wishes on Tuesday to hear the views of parliament on these very important international problems which face us today. It is very necessary, as the Leader of the Opposition said in his opening speech, that the discussion should take place at an early date. Then, when the request was subsequently made by the hon. member for Vancouver East we naturally fell into line and it is our intention to proceed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
